title: Play and amusement
hook: this life is play, amusement, adornment, boasting, and rivalry in wealth (57:20)

segments.voice: Yesterday, khushu', and your line was has the time not come? Did you take your one small step? Day six hundred fourteen.

A toddler with a plastic bucket on the beach. A teenager scrolling at midnight. A thirty-year-old choosing the right outfit for a wedding. A forty-year-old mentioning, casually, the new car. A seventy-year-old counting grandchildren and property. Line them up and it looks like five different people wanting five different things. Surah Al-Hadid, verse twenty, lines up five words in a row. Some commentators have read them as exactly that: one life, seen from the beach to the end.

Pickthall: "Know that the life of the world is only play, and idle talk, and pageantry, and boasting among you, and rivalry in respect of wealth and children". In Arabic, the five are la'ib, play; lahw, amusement or diversion; zina, adornment; tafakhur, boasting to one another; and takathur, piling up more wealth and children than the next person. Some commentators noticed the order follows the stages of a life: the child plays, the youth is diverted, the young adult adorns, the grown person boasts, the old person counts what they've gathered. Then the verse gives a picture. It's like rain that brings up plants that delight the farmer. Then they dry, and you see them turn yellow, then they become straw. Green, yellow, straw. That's the life of the world, in one season. And then, in the next verse, a turn: race one another toward forgiveness from your Lord, and a garden as wide as the heavens and the earth. Is the verse against fun? The hadith collections suggest not. Bukhari records that the Prophet ﷺ let 'A'isha watch a group of Abyssinians performing with spears in the mosque on a feast day, standing so she could see over his shoulder until she'd had enough. The verse isn't banning the beach bucket. It's naming what play is: lovely, and passing, like grass after rain. The verse's warning is against mistaking it for the whole of life.
screen: `PLAY, AMUSEMENT, ADORNMENT.` · `BOASTING, AND PILING UP MORE.` · `GREEN, YELLOW, STRAW.` · `RACE TOWARD FORGIVENESS.`

segments.voice: The practice: put down one amusement for an hour. Sit, and breathe. Think of the thing that most often fills your spare minutes: a game, a feed, a show, a habit of checking. You don't need to judge it. Just picture setting it down for one hour today. Picture what might fill that hour instead: a walk, a person, a page, a prayer if you pray. Then let the picture rest, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Lahw: amusement, diversion, one of the five words Surah Al-Hadid uses for the passing life of the world. Today's word.
Your line: play passes. Today, put your one amusement down for an hour, and notice what that hour turns into. Day six hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: Muslim preachers often recite 57:20 in reminders about the passing nature of worldly life, while the hadith tradition also preserves room for play, sport and celebration, especially on the two Eids.

fork.reveal: he let her watch, standing so she could see, until she'd had enough. the verse names play as passing, not forbidden.

original.note: Arabic: play and amusement, the first two of the five words of 57:20.

trapdoor: what you thought: a verse saying fun is bad.
what it means: a verse naming what play is, lovely and passing, and pointing beyond it.
what a scholar hears: five nouns read by some commentators as life's stages; the vegetation parable; 57:21's 'race toward forgiveness'; and the play of the Abyssinians in Bukhari as a counterweight.
